Article Title: ‘Congress part of every conspiracy’: CM Yogi hits out at opposition amid 'dissent within EC' row
Article Text:
Yogi Adityanath hits out at opposition over SIR row

NEW DELHI: Uttar Pradesh chief minister Yogi Adityanath defended the Election Commission amid the "dissent within the poll body" row, while slamming the Congress party for "creating confusion and targeting constitutional institutions".Tearing into the rival Congress for criticisng the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls, the Uttar Pradesh CM said: "The current SIR exercise was not the first such revision undertaken by the Election Commission, pointing to similar exercises conducted in 1952, 1957, 1961, 1965–66 and 2003.""Regarding the SIR (Special Intensive Revision), the confusion that has been consistently created by them (opposition parties), it is not as if the current Election Commission is the first to undertake such an exercise; in the past—often under Congress-led governments—similar exercises were conducted in 1952, 1957, 1961, 1965–66, and even in 2003. Despite this history, the uproar raised by the Congress, Samajwadi Party, RJD, and other parties over the current SIR exercise is extremely unfortunate. "He said the Election Commission had already clarified that eligible voters who were left out would be given an opportunity to submit the required form. He also referred to the Supreme Court’s position on the Election Commission’s action regarding Form 6."All three Election Commissioners came before the press and clarified the situation.Regarding SIR, directions had already been issued that all eligible voters who were left out would be given an opportunity to fill the form. The Supreme Court has also upheld the Election Commission's action regarding Form 6. Despite this, putting the Election Commission and Chief Election Commissioners in the dock, questioning every constitutional institution and attempting to tarnish India's image globally is extremely unfortunate. Congress and its allies should control their irresponsible actions. There should be no place for violence, vandalism or misinformation in a democracy."Adityanath further accused the Congress and other opposition parties of undermining constitutional institutions and democratic values for political interests."The approach of the Congress and opposition parties has always been to be a part of every conspiracy to harm the constitutional institutions of India and weaken the democratic values ​​for their political interests, due to which the world's largest democracy can be harmed. It is surprising that the current actions and rhetoric of the country's main opposition party and other parties associated with the UPA alliance are extremely irresponsible and damaging to democratic values. "Adityanath also criticised the Congress over its objections to EVMs, noting that Congress governments had been formed at the Centre and in several states through elections conducted using the machines. He linked the criticism to what he described as a broader pattern of questioning democratic institutions."The EVMs, through which Congress governments have also been formed at the Centre and in several states, have been called a black box, raising questions about India's electoral system and the country's democratic values. Recall that on June 25, 1975, Congress sinned by undermining the Constitution by imposing the Emergency. Congress-led governments also repeatedly dismissed elected governments of opposition parties through unconstitutional means. Their actions have repeatedly compromised the country's internal and external security. Questioning the valour of the Indian armed forces during the Balakot airstrike and attempting to cast doubt on the bravery of Indian soldiers during Operation Sindoor are examples of this approach."The remarks come amid a major political confrontation over reported objections raised by two Election Commissioners to decisions related to the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls. Opposition parties have demanded action against Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar, an immediate halt to the SIR exercise and fresh elections in states where polls have already been held.The ruling BJP, however, defended the Election Commission, saying differences expressed by Election Commissioners during internal deliberations demonstrated that the poll panel was functioning democratically rather than under a “dictatorial” system
Article Summary: Yogi adityanath hits out at opposition over sir row. Uttar pradesh chief minister slams the congress party for "creating confusion and targeting constitutional institutions" opposition parties have demanded action against chief election commissioner gyanesh kumar. The ruling bjp, however, defended the election commission.

Article Title: As Trump hugs Xi and plugs Sharif, India feels the squeeze
Article Text:
Trump’s outreach to Xi and praise for Sharif come as India faces a more transactional US relationship

TOI correspondent from Washington:

The clearest sign yet of a widening US-India diplomatic rift came this weekend from the White House and the United Nations, where India was denouncing Pakistan for what it called a litany of “falsehoods” and “deceit,” even as US President Donald Trump appeared to give those very claims a presidential imprimatur.Pakistan Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif had used his UN General Assembly address to revive Islamabad’s account of the 2025 India-Pakistan conflict, crediting Trump with a “timely intervention” that, he said, prevented a wider war. On Friday night, shortly after China’s President Xi Jinping had departed for Beijing, Trump posted an 87-second excerpt of Sharif’s speech on Truth Social without comment. The clip included Sharif’s praise of Trump and Pakistan Army chief Asim Munir.The timing was striking. India had just exercised its Right of Reply, with First Secretary Petal Gahlot accusing Islamabad of peddling “falsehoods” and “deceit” and describing Pakistan as a “puppet” regime. New Delhi has also rejected Trump’s repeated assertion that he mediated the cessation of hostilities in May 2025, saying the fighting was halted after direct military-to-military communication between India and Pakistan.For India, however, the larger concern may be less about one Truth Social post than about a pattern. The Xi visit to Washington this week appeared to underscore how dramatically the strategic geometry of US foreign policy has shifted. Rather than organizing its Asia policy principally around building India as a counterweight to China – a two-decade old Washington objective that resulting in an “Indo-Pacific” focused QUAD – the Trump White House increasingly appears willing to deal with Beijing as a peer whose cooperation is indispensable, and whose confrontation carries costs Trump is reluctant to incur.Following the Xi visit, Washington and Beijing extended their trade truce and agreed on tariff reductions covering $30 billion of less-sensitive goods in each direction, according reports in the Chinese media. They also operationalized bilateral boards on trade and investment and agreed to pursue an artificial-intelligence dialogue.Analysts say none of this amounts to a formal US-China condominium, and deep disagreements over Taiwan, technology, trade and strategic competition remain. But the emerging arrangement has prompted comparisons with a de facto G-2: Washington and Beijing managing their rivalry directly while other powers, including India, find themselves having to adjust to decisions made in a room in which they are not present.“One totally unsurprising consequence of this US-China trade truce is that Trump is not even thinking about implementing the Lindsey Graham Russia sanctions legislation he just signed, which would have required penalizing China's support for Russia's war machine,” Tom Malinowski a former New Jersey lawmaker noted, even as Republicans close to Trump have been champing at the bit to punish New Delhi. The Graham bill, signed by Trump on Sept. 18, gives the president authority to impose tariffs of up to 100% on countries that continue buying Russian crude or natural gas under specified conditions. The law specifically covers countries among the five largest Russian oil or gas importers that make new purchases, as well as countries identified among the top facilitators of sanctions evasion.India is plainly exposed to that provision, as is China. Yet the contrast in Trump’s handling of the two relationships has become difficult for New Delhi to ignore: Beijing is being courted into a new economic accommodation even as India faces the prospect of punitive trade action.The message was reinforced this week by a senior State Department official who said the Graham law gives Trump “a new tool in his toolbox,” while emphasizing that its use is not automatic. The official pointed to a broad national-security waiver but added that Washington expects India to help the US end the Ukraine war.More revealing was the official's description of what Washington now wants from India: not necessarily strategic alignment against China, but access to the enormous Indian energy market. “We are looking to also become a huge source of India's energy needs,” the official was quoted as saying, pointing to expanding US hydrocarbon exports and urging faster diversification away from Russian supplies.All this is consequential because for two decades the bipartisan American strategy had been to help India acquire the economic, military and technological heft to balance China's rise. As recently as May, Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who will be back in New Delhi in October, was describing India as one of America's most important strategic partners, while US officials continued to characterize New Delhi as a critical Indo-Pacific counterweight.The language now coming from Washington is noticeably more transactional.For New Delhi, the resulting unease is not simply about tariffs or Pakistan. It is about whether a strategic partnership painstakingly built across successive administrations is being replaced by a transactional relationship in which China is too powerful to punish, Pakistan is useful to cultivate, and India is expected to accommodate. And as New Delhi watched Washington kiss up to Beijing as an indispensable peer and embrace a country New Delhi views as a terrorism sponsor, the strategic space India once occupied in the American imagination appeared to be shrinking.
Article Summary: Trump’s outreach to xi and praise for sharif come as india faces a more transactional us relationship. New delhi has also rejected trump's repeated assertion that he mediated the cessation of hostilities in may 2025. The emerging arrangement has prompted comparisons with a de facto g-2: washington and beijing managing their rivalry directly.

Article Title: India's right to defend itself from terrorism will be exercised: EAM
Article Text:
EAM S Jaishankar

Describing Pakistan as a serial practitioner of terrorism in his UNGA address, foreign minister S Jaishankar said that there must be no dilution of the zero-tolerance approach to the menace. Without naming Pakistan PM Shehbaz Sharif, who had raked up the Kashmir issue in his General Assembly speech on Friday, Jaishankar said he had misrepresented facts and invoked arguments to normalise terrorism and claim immunity from its consequences."That will not stand," said the minister, adding that the scourge of terrorism had been a persistent threat to peace.Jaishankar called state-sponsored terrorism with a cross-border purpose a direct challenge to the global order, adding that India's right to defend itself from terrorism will be exercised.In his remarks, Sharif had yet again given credit to US President Donald Trump for ending the India-Pakistan conflict last year with his "timely intervention"."Govts indulging in such practices must be held accountable. There must be no dilution in our zero-tolerance approach towards terrorism. Its financial aspects, in particular, should be exposed and should be countered," said Jaishankar."Friendship and goodwill cannot co-exist with terrorism.And understandings premised on that will naturally be called into question. It is for the perpetrator of terrorism to mend its ways," he added.He also flagged the need to end conflicts in West Asia and Ukraine, saying the inability to maintain peace is not just undermining security but threatening progress and retarding development. "In a globalised world, the effects of war are felt worldwide. Countries far from conflicts are being penalised for no fault of theirs. Those most impacted often have the least say.""The targeting of commercial shipping and seafarers transiting international waterways is simply unacceptable," he said. Speaking on the West Asia crisis, the minister backed the two-state solution for durable and lasting peace.Jaishankar spoke about the Global South predicament in today's world and also the misuse of AI. He said a mindset of extreme competition had set in, undermining institutions and establishing choke points."Global South's right to industrialise is also undermined by non-market practices and market denial. The march of technology that was meant to instill hope has now become a source of anxiety. Misuse of AI is sharpening bias and diluting mutual respect. These directions bode ill for the aims and objectives of the UN."
Article Summary: Eam s jaishankar called state-sponsored terrorism with a cross-border purpose a direct challenge to the global order. Without naming pakistan pm shehbaz sharif, he said he had misrepresented facts and invoked arguments to normalise terrorism and claim immunity from its consequences.

NEW DELHI: Elections are, by their very nature, a contest.Political parties fight for ground, candidates wage fierce campaigns and voters ultimately decide whom to trust with their mandate.Through it all, the Election Commission is meant to stand apart and monitor the process. Its role is to frame the rules, enforce them fairly and ensure that the contest remains even-handed.Yet, in recent days, the spotlight has moved away from those fighting the election and towards the institution meant to referee it.The players are no longer the only ones under scrutiny. Increasingly, the referee itself has become the subject of the debate.A report in The Indian Express claimed that Election Commissioners Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi repeatedly raised objections with Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar over decisions and communications that they said were issued without their knowledge or approval.The Election Commission has rejected the suggestion that the episode points to a breakdown in its functioning. It has maintained that differences of opinion are a normal part of institutional deliberation and that all final decisions of the Commission have been unanimous.That leaves a larger constitutional question at the heart of the controversy: how is India's election watchdog actually supposed to function?Is the Chief Election Commissioner the boss of the Election Commission, or simply the first among three equals? What happens when the three commissioners disagree? And why has the law governing their appointment become a subject of such intense controversy?On September 23, The Indian Express reported that Sandhu and Joshi had, on multiple occasions, objected to decisions and communications they said were taken or issued without their prior knowledge.According to the report, the two commissioners recorded such objections on at least 14 occasions over the past 10 months.The issues reportedly ranged from changes to electoral forms and access to the voter database to the allocation of work within the Commission and the filing of appeals involving electoral rolls.The report has since triggered a wider debate over whether the Election Commission's three members are exercising their powers collectively, as the law envisages, or whether the CEC has acquired a greater role in practice.According to the Indian Express report, the concerns raised by Sandhu and Joshi covered several aspects of the Commission's functioning.Taken together, the reported objections raise a question that goes beyond any individual decision: how does a three-member constitutional body exercise collective authority when its members do not initially agree?The Election Commission strongly rejected the suggestion that its internal differences amount to a breakdown in decision-making, and added that all official orders and administrative directions had been issued unanimously."Differing views and observations are a normal part of deliberation in any institution. They are a part of the decision-making process before a final decision is taken. Not only the three Commissioners, but every officer of the Commission is fully authorised to give his suggestions to the Commission for improving the electoral system," the ECI said in a statement."In recent months, the Commission has taken numerous decisions, issued instructions, introduced around 40 new initiatives and undertaken many electoral reforms, including the conduct of electoral roll revision (including SIR) across the country. All these decisions are an outcome of the unanimous decisions of the full Commission in the past one year," the poll body added.It also criticised the media report, saying that highlighting specific internal notes over a period of 10 months gives only one part of the picture."Highlighting certain specific internal notes/observations spread over the period of 10 months while overlooking the much larger body of approvals, decisions, instructions and initiatives give only one part of the picture," it said.The disagreement, therefore, is not simply over whether commissioners have expressed reservations. It is over what those reservations mean for the functioning of the institution as a whole.This is where the 2023 law becomes important.Section 18 of the Chief Election Commissioner and Other Election Commissioners Act, 2023, provides that the Commission may, by unanimous decision, regulate how its business is conducted and allocate work among the CEC and the other Election Commissioners.It also says that, as far as possible, the Commission's business should be transacted unanimously.But it makes an important provision for situations in which consensus is not possible.If the CEC and the other Election Commissioners differ on a matter, the issue is to be decided according to the opinion of the majority.In other words, the statutory framework does not make the CEC an executive superior to the other two commissioners. The three constitute the Commission collectively, while the CEC is the "first among equals".The CEC can have a distinct role within the institution, but the law does not provide for a system in which the CEC's view automatically prevails over the other two commissioners.Where the three disagree, the majority view is the deciding view.The controversy now centres on whether some of the decisions cited in the recent report were, in practice, implemented despite objections from the other two commissioners, and if so, how that squares with the statutory scheme governing the Commission's decision-making.The current controversy also brings back an older and deeper question: Who should appoint the people who conduct India's elections?In March 2023, the Supreme Court ruled that Parliament had not yet enacted a law governing appointments to the Election Commission, despite Article 324 of the Constitution envisaging such a framework.Until Parliament enacted such a law, a Constitution bench prescribed an interim selection mechanism comprising the Prime Minister, the Leader of Opposition in the Lok Sabha and the Chief Justice of India.The court stressed that an independent Election Commission was essential for democracy and observed that those entrusted with conducting elections must be insulated from executive influence.Parliament subsequently enacted the Chief Election Commissioner and Other Election Commissioners (Appointment, Conditions of Service and Term of Office) Act, 2023.But the new law changed the composition of the selection committee.Instead of the Chief Justice of India, it provided for a Union Cabinet minister nominated by the Prime Minister. The committee therefore consists of the Prime Minister, a Union minister nominated by him and the Leader of Opposition in the Lok Sabha.The opposition has alleged that the 2023 Act gives the executive “overwhelming” control over the appointment of Election Commissioners. The government, meanwhile, has defended the law and its institutional framework.The dispute has now reached the Supreme Court, where a challenge to the validity of the appointment law produced a split verdict.A two-judge SC bench differed over whether the matter should immediately be referred to a Constitution bench. Justices Dipankar Datta and Satish Chandra Sharma disagreed on that question, although both agreed that the matter should ultimately be placed before the Chief Justice of India for consideration by a larger bench.They also agreed that sending the case first to a three-judge bench would be of "little worth" and could further delay a final determination of the constitutional questions involved. The matter is likely to be heard by a 5-judge bench soon.The issue is vital as it extends beyond the current dispute inside the Election Commission. It touches a larger institutional question: How independent should the body conducting India's elections be from the executive, and what safeguards should govern the appointment of those who head it?The latest controversy has also acquired a political dimension, with opposition parties preparing fresh notices seeking the removal of CEC Gyanesh Kumar.According to media reports, the notices, being drafted and vetted by experts, are expected to be submitted in the Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha next week. The proposed notices are expected to include issues raised in the Indian Express report.This would not be the opposition's first attempt.On April 7, Lok Sabha Speaker Om Birla and Rajya Sabha Chairperson CP Radhakrishnan rejected an earlier notice seeking Kumar's removal. That notice had been signed by 130 Lok Sabha members and 63 Rajya Sabha members and alleged partisanship and arbitrariness in the conduct of the SIR exercise.Separately, a notice submitted by 73 opposition MPs in the Rajya Sabha on April 24 seeking Kumar's removal remains pending in the Upper House.But removing a CEC is deliberately difficult.Article 324(5) of the Constitution provides that the Chief Election Commissioner can be removed only "in like manner and on the like grounds as a Judge of the Supreme Court".The same protection is incorporated into Section 11(2) of the 2023 Act.The other Election Commissioners enjoy a different safeguard: they cannot be removed from office except on the recommendation of the CEC.The higher threshold for removing a CEC is intended to protect the office from arbitrary or politically motivated removal.The removal process is rooted in the constitutional procedure applicable to Supreme Court judges.Article 124(4) of the Constitution, which lays down the procedure for removing a Supreme Court judge, states that a judge can be removed only by an order of the President following an address by each House of Parliament.Such an address must be supported by a majority of the total membership of that House and by a majority of at least two-thirds of members present and voting, in the same session, on the ground of proved misbehaviour or incapacity.The process begins with a notice of motion in either House of Parliament alleging misbehaviour or incapacity. The notice must be signed by at least 100 MPs in the Lok Sabha or 50 MPs in the Rajya Sabha.The presiding officer of the concerned House can admit or refuse the motion after considering the material and information available. If the motion is admitted, an inquiry is conducted into the charges by a committee constituted for the purpose.If the charges are established, the motion must be passed by a majority of the total membership of each House and by a two-thirds majority of members present and voting in both Houses.Once both Houses pass the motion in accordance with these requirements, an address is made to the President, who then issues the order removing the CEC.The President's role at this stage is constitutional and formal once Parliament has passed the required address.The current structure of the Election Commission is itself the product of an institutional evolution.When the ECI was established in 1950, it was a single-member body, with the Chief Election Commissioner as its sole member.It became a three-member body for the first time in 1989, but that arrangement was short-lived. In January 1990, the VP Singh government reverted the Commission to a single-member structure.The system changed again in October 1993, when the PV Narasimha Rao government appointed MS Gill and GVG Krishnamurthy as Election Commissioners alongside CEC TN Seshan.Seshan challenged the appointments in the Supreme Court, arguing that the addition of commissioners diluted the authority of the CEC.In its 1995 judgment, a Constitution bench upheld the multi-member structure.The court made clear that the CEC was not institutionally superior to the other Election Commissioners. The three were intended to function collectively, with differences being resolved through the decision-making mechanism of the Commission.That judgment established the broad institutional framework that exists today.The Election Commission is not designed as a hierarchy in which one person commands and two others merely assist. Nor is it simply three independent offices operating in parallel. It is a constitutional body meant to function collectively.The law provides for unanimity where possible and a majority where consensus fails.The CEC occupies the position of first among equals, rather than that of a superior authority.The significance of the current controversy, therefore, lies not merely in the existence of disagreements within the Commission. Differences are inevitable in any institution exercising such enormous constitutional responsibility.The larger question is what happens after those differences arise: whether they remain part of an internal deliberative process, as the ECI maintains, or whether they reflect a deeper dispute over how collective authority is being exercised.The credibility of an election does not rest only on the final tally of votes.It also rests on whether voters believe that the rules were applied fairly, the institutions enforcing them remained above the contest and the process was conducted without favour or hidden influence.The Election Commission, therefore, carries a burden that goes beyond administering polls: it must command confidence across the political spectrum and among voters themselves. Any perception that the referee is divided, opaque or partisan can cast a shadow over the process, even when the electoral machinery continues to function formally within the law.In the end, public trust is not built merely by declaring an election free and fair; it is built by ensuring that voters have little reason to doubt that verdict.
Article Summary: The cec can have a distinct role within the institution, but the law does not provide for a system in which the cec's view automatically prevails over the other two commissioners. The two commissioners reportedly objected to changes made to form 6 without following due process.

Article Title: Higher EPF wage limit: Monthly PF contributions rise to Rs 3,917
Article Text:
EPFO wage ceiling hike

NEW DELHI: With EPFO increasing the mandatory wage ceiling from Rs 15,000 a month to Rs 25,000, employees will now contribute Rs 3,000 (at 12% contribution of Rs 25,000 wage) towards their PF savings from Rs 1,800 earlier, govt said in a set of FAQs released. This will be along with a contribution of Rs 917 by employers (at 3.67%), up from Rs 550, taking the mandatory monthly PF contributions to Rs 3,917.In addition, Rs 2,083 - an 8.3% contribution from employers' share - will now go towards the pension kitty from earlier Rs 1,250. On Sept 17, govt increased EPFO wage ceiling to bring one crore additional workers into the social security net as minimum wages in at least seven states and UTs - Delhi, Maharashtra, Karnataka, Haryana, Gujarat, Rajasthan and Uttarakhand - have crossed the Rs 15,000 threshold.In the case of an employee with a monthly wage of Rs 20,000, the mandatory PF contribution will be Rs 3,134 - the employee share Rs 2,400 and the employer share Rs 734, with an additional Rs 1,666 going towards EPS from employer's share. But if an employee earns, say, Rs 35,000 a month, the mandatory PF contribution will be Rs 6,000 (Rs 3,000 from employee and employers each), with no amount going towards pension as EPS is available only to those whose wages do not exceed the EPFO wage ceiling.The retirement savings agency said the new regime kicked in from Sept 17 and asked employers to review contractor compliance, wherever contract labour is engaged, and update its payroll systems.Allaying employee fears of attempts to pass on the contribution by deducting more from salaries, it said an employer's statutory contribution cannot simply be treated as an employee deduction merely by describing it as part of CTC.While the move will likely increase compliance costs for small and medium enterprises, the potential costs due to the rise in the wage ceiling can be partly offset by the incentive of up to Rs 3,000 per month for every additional employment created under PM Viksit Bharat Rojgar Yojana.
Article Summary: Epfo increasing mandatory wage ceiling from rs 15,000 a month to rs 25,000. Employees will now contribute rs 3,000 towards their pf savings from rs 1,800 earlier. This will be along with a contribution of rs 917 by employers (at 3.67%), up from rs 550.

Article Title: India, Canada seek to take ties ‘to a higher level’: EAM Jaishankar after UNGA meet
Article Text:
EAM S Jaishankar during a meeting with Canadanian counterpart Anita Anand on the UNGA sidelines.

Modi visit and trade deal in focus

Jaishankar holds more bilateral meetings

NEW DELHI: India and Canada are looking to take their bilateral relationship to a “higher level”, external affairs minister S Jaishankar said after meeting Canadian Foreign Minister Anita Anand on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly.“Always a pleasure to meet FM @AnitaAnandMP of Canada #UNGA81 A productive discussion as we prepare to take the relationship to a higher level,” Jaishankar said in a post on X on Saturday.The meeting comes as New Delhi and Ottawa work to rebuild ties and advance negotiations for a Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement. The two sides have set a target of concluding the trade negotiations by the end of 2026.Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said earlier this week that he expected Prime Minister Narendra Modi to visit Canada in December. He also said negotiations on the trade agreement were making “good progress”.“We are making good progress in our trade negotiations with India. It is an exceptionally important relationship on many many levels, people-to-people levels, security levels, and also trade and economic,” Carney said at a press conference on the sidelines of the UNGA.Carney was responding to questions about Modi's possible visit and the timeline for the trade agreement.Canada had formally invited Modi to visit in 2026, with both governments agreeing to work through diplomatic channels to settle a mutually convenient date.The possible December visit could coincide with the G20 Summit in Miami, which US President Donald Trump is scheduled to host on December 14 and 15.India and Canada have been working to broaden cooperation beyond trade, including in energy, critical minerals, technology, defence and talent. The two countries have also agreed to work towards a stronger strategic partnership.Jaishankar also met Venezuelan Foreign Minister Felix Plasencia Gonzalez during the UNGA. After the meeting, he said, “Our energy ties are gaining momentum, besides other areas of bilateral cooperation. We also discussed current regional issues.”The meeting comes as India looks to diversify its energy supplies and strengthen relationships with oil-producing countries.Jaishankar also held talks with Belarusian Foreign Minister Maxim Ryzhenkov and Mexican Foreign Minister Roberto Velasco Alvarez on the sidelines of the UNGA.
Article Summary: S jaishankar met canadian foreign minister anita anand on the sidelines of the un general assembly. The meeting comes as new delhi and ottawa work to rebuild ties and advance negotiations for a comprehensive economic partnership agreement.

NEW DELHI: India has called for a global system that ensures countries sharing pathogens and biological resources during a health emergency also get timely access to vaccines, diagnostics, medicines and technologies developed from them.The demand was made at the UN High-Level Meeting on Pandemic Prevention, Preparedness and Response in New York, where India stressed that the credibility of the WHO Pandemic Agreement would depend on a fair Pathogen Access and Benefit Sharing (PABS) system.Union health secretary Punya Salila Srivastava said countries contributing pathogens should receive the benefits arising from their use, while respecting national sovereignty. She also said ongoing negotiations on the PABS system should not be prejudged and that implementation should take into account national circumstances and capacities.Drawing on its experience during Covid-19, India also called for digital public infrastructure to be recognised as a global public good, citing its role in disease surveillance, vaccination, risk communication, supply chains and continuity of health services during the pandemic.India highlighted its contribution during Covid, saying it supplied 300 million vaccine doses to around 100 countries and two UN entities, besides providing medical assistance to more than 150 countries.At the meeting, India also outlined measures to strengthen pandemic preparedness, including expanding laboratory networks, emergency coordination, the health workforce, stockpiles and clinical care capacity.The WHO Pandemic Agreement, adopted in May 2025, is aimed at strengthening global preparedness for future pandemics. WHO Director-General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus called for urgent completion of negotiations on the PABS system, saying delays could affect the world's ability to respond to future pandemics.India stressed that pandemic preparedness must remain rooted in national health systems and domestic financing, with international assistance complementing national efforts. It also called for equity and global solidarity to remain central to preparations for future outbreaks.

NEW DELHI: Union minister Prahlad Joshi on Saturday hit out at the opposition over its protest against Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar amid the ongoing controversy surrounding the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls, saying there was no “concrete proof” to support the allegations being raised against the Election Commission.Reacting to the opposition's claims, Joshi said the protest was an expression of the “pain” caused by its electoral defeat. He said the SIR issue was being used to voice that distress.“The pain in their hearts caused by their defeat... they are trying to express that distress through the SIR issue,” Joshi said.His remarks came in response to questions about a report published by The Indian Express, which cited concerns allegedly raised within the Election Commission over the SIR exercise. The report claimed that Election Commissioners Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi had raised 14 written dissents or objections over a 10-month period.The reports led the opposition to seek action against CEC Gyanesh Kumar and demand a halt to the SIR, while the ECI said internal notes, queries and differences of view are part of its functioning and maintained that all final decisions on the exercise were unanimous.Joshi said that even if the report was taken into consideration, it did not amount to conclusive evidence of wrongdoing.“Whatever has appeared in The Indian Express... if you even believe that, I am not saying they have no right, but I am also saying that it is not concrete proof for that. It is not at all concrete proof,” he said.Joshi also disputed the opposition's suggestion that decisions related to the SIR were taken unilaterally. Referring to the Election Commission's own press release, he said decisions of the poll panel had been unanimous.“And whatever has been written in The Indian Express, even that never states that a unilateral decision was taken. All the decisions—all, I am not saying almost—all the decisions of the Election Commission have been taken unanimously,” Joshi said.The Union minister, however, clarified that he was not speaking on behalf of the poll panel.“I am not talking on behalf of the Election Commission, but I am speaking based on the press release issued by the Election Commission,” Joshi said.The opposition has been protesting against CEC Gyanesh Kumar over the SIR exercise and has raised questions about the manner in which the electoral-roll revision is being conducted.
Article Summary: Union minister prahlad joshi hit out at the opposition over its protest against chief election commissioner gyanesh kumar. He said there was no “concrete proof” to support the allegations being raised against the election commission. Joshi said the protest was an expression of the “pain” caused by its electoral defeat.

Pakistan Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif's address at the United Nations General Assembly, in which he sought to reiterate Islamabad's false narrative on the 2025 conflict with India, drew a viral reaction from an Indian diplomat.The cameras captured Indian diplomat R Srinivas appearing to smirk and laugh as Sharif spoke about Pakistan’s claimed “victory” in the May 2025 conflict with India.The moment came as Sharif presented Islamabad’s version of the conflict and raised several issues concerning India, including the Indus Waters Treaty and Kashmir.Addressing the UN, Sharif praised US President Donald Trump for his role in preventing further escalation between the two nuclear-armed neighbours during Operation Sindoor “His timely intervention came at a decisive juncture when two nuclear-armed neighbours stood at the brink of an all-out war. And, who knows, Mr President, the extent of devastation that could have taken place had President Trump not stepped in at this critical moment with clarity of thought and action,” Sharif said.“Mr President, we must therefore ensure that South Asia never reaches that precipice ever again,” he added.India, however, has consistently maintained that the cessation of military action on May 10, 2025, was reached through direct communication between India and Pakistan and did not involve third-party mediation.Pakistan’s Director General of Military Operations (DGMO) had approached his Indian counterpart on May 10, seeking a cessation of military action.India had launched Operation Sindoor on May 7, 2025, following the April 22 Pahalgam terror attack that killed 26 people. India said the operation targeted terrorist infrastructure in Pakistan and Pakistan-occupied Jammu and Kashmir.India also exercised its right of reply to Sharif’s remarks. Petal Gahlot, First Secretary in India’s Permanent Mission to the UN, criticised Pakistan’s political system and its references to democratic rights and human values. She also referred to Osama bin Laden’s presence near Pakistan’s military academy.“This afternoon, the General Assembly heard some bizarre remarks from the representative of Pakistan. This happens just a fortnight after New York City and the world marked the 25th anniversary of the horrendous 9-11 terrorist attack. This context is important to keep in mind because its mastermind, Osama bin Laden, was living right on the doorstep of the Pakistani Army's premier academy. This was the very entity which was the subject of such deep genuflection before us today by the representative of Pakistan. But all this is only to be expected from what Pakistanis themselves call a Form 47 government.”Gahlot also responded to Pakistan’s references to democratic rights and the role of the military in the country. “We heard some hypocritical homilies about democratic rights and human values from a regime whose capital at this very moment is being fortified against its own people. And that, Mr. President, is happening because this is a regime of the army, by the army, and for the army.Their puppets may come and go, but let us have no illusion about who calls the shots. The reality of Pakistan is expressed in its 27th Amendment and the lifelong immunity granted to its real ruler," she added.Sharif also criticised India’s decision to place the Indus Waters Treaty in abeyance, arguing that the “move was not legal” and highlighting the importance of the Indus river system to Pakistan.India placed the treaty in abeyance following the Pahalgam terror attack and has said the decision will remain in effect until Pakistan takes credible and irreversible action against cross-border terrorism. The 1960 Indus Waters Treaty governs the sharing of the waters of the Indus river system between India and Pakistan.
Article Summary: Pak pm sharif praises us president donald trump. Indian diplomat r srinivas appears to smirk and laugh as sharif spoke about pakistan’s claimed ‘victory’ in the may 2025 conflict with india. India has consistently maintained that the cessation of military action on may 10, 2025, was reached through direct communication between india and pakistan.

NEW DELHI: Bharatiya Janata Party on Saturday took a jibe at Mamata Banerjee's reported outreach to the CPM amid the ongoing row over the Election Commission, saying the former chief minister was trying to find a role in the opposition INDIA bloc after losing power in the state.Speaking to reporters, West Bengal minister Dilip Ghosh said CPM leaders had earlier tried to reach out to Mamata, but she had never spoken to them. He said the political equations had now changed."Earlier, when they would call Mamata Banerjee, she never spoke to them. Now the situation is reversed. She seems to be approaching them or expecting a call from them," the West Bengal minister said."As she has no role here, she is trying to play a role somewhere else," he added.The ongoing row over the Election Commission has brought West Bengal's bitter political rivals, the Mamata Banerjee-led TMC and the CPM, on the same page.CPM general secretary M A Baby spoke to Mamata, who agreed that the situation warranted coordinated action.Meanwhile, INDIA bloc parties are likely to meet in New Delhi on September 30 to discuss concerns over the Election Commission and the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls, besides other issues, news agency PTI reported, citing sources.The proposed meeting comes amid increased coordination among opposition parties over the Election Commission, following reports of differences within the poll panel over aspects of the SIR exercise.Opposition parties are also working on a fresh removal notice against CEC Gyanesh Kumar, which is likely to be submitted in both Houses of Parliament after being vetted by legal experts. It would be the third such attempt by the opposition.The latest mobilisation follows an Indian Express report that Election Commissioners Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi had raised objections on several occasions over decisions and orders related to the SIR.The Election Commission has said that differing views and observations are a normal part of institutional deliberations and asserted that its orders have full legal sanction and follow statutory procedures.
Article Summary: West bengal minister dilip ghosh said cpm leaders had earlier tried to reach out to mamata, but she had never spoken to them. He said the political equations had now changed. "as she has no role here, she is trying to play a role somewhere else," he added.
